source_text: His peractis Machabaico gaudio Mariani mater exultans et passione perfecta iam secura de filio, non illi tantum coeperat, sed et sibi, quae tale pignus ediderat, gratulari. Conplectebatur in filii corpore suorum uiscerum gloriam, et in ipsa ceruicis uulnera frequens osculum pietas religiosa figebat. O te merito Mariam! O te beatam et filio tuo, mater, et nomine! Quis in ea tanti uocabuli felicitatem aliquando credat errasse, quam sic uteri sui fetus ornauit? Inaestimabilis uere dei omnipotentis et Christi eius in suos misericordia, qui fidentes in suum nomen non solum gratiae dignatione confortat, sed et sanguinis redemptione uiuificat. Nam quis digna aestimatione possit eius beneficia metiri? Qui in hoc quoque paterna indulgentia semper operatur, ut in nos et hoc ipsum, quod in nostro sanguine rependi credimus, conferatur ab omnipotente deo; cui est gloria in saecula saeculorum, amen.
thought_title: A Mother Rejoicing Over Her Son
orientation: The narrator closes the account after the beheading by the river outside the city, with the mother of Marian embracing his body.
pass_a_gloss: These things having been done, exulting with Maccabean joy and now secure about her son because his suffering was complete, the mother of Marian had begun to congratulate not him only but also herself, who had brought forth such a pledge. She was embracing in the body of her son the glory of her own inward parts, and religious devotion was pressing a repeated kiss on the very wounds of the neck. O you rightly Mary! O you blessed, mother, both by your son and by your name! Who could believe that the good fortune of so great a name ever went astray in her, whom the child of her womb so adorned? Truly inestimable is the mercy of almighty God and of his Christ toward his own, who strengthens those trusting in his name not only by gracious favor but also gives life by redemption of blood. For who could measure his benefits with worthy reckoning? He always works with fatherly indulgence even in this, that even this very thing, which we believe is paid back in our blood, is bestowed upon us by almighty God, to whom is glory for ages of ages, amen.

lemmas.gloss: to be paid back, repaid here

choices.why: keeps the source allusion to the mother in 2 Maccabees 7 without treating it as a formal citation
literal sense of pignus for a child brought forth, keeps the legal pledge image
subject of figebat, abstract devotion acting, not the mother herself
vocative wordplay on her name Mariam matching Mary mother language in the next clause
required glossary English for dignatio as Gods gracious favor permitting suffering

pass_b_english: When all this was finished, Marian's mother rejoiced with Maccabean joy. His passion was complete, and she was at peace about her son at last. She congratulated not only him but herself too, for bringing such a pledge into the world.

She embraced in her son's body the glory of her own womb, and religious devotion pressed kiss after kiss on the wounds of his neck. O you rightly Mary! O mother, blessed both in your son and in your name! Who could ever think the good fortune of so great a name had missed its mark in her, when she adorned the child of her womb like this?

Truly beyond reckoning is the mercy of almighty God and of his Christ toward his own. He strengthens those who trust in his name not only by gracious favor but also gives them life by redemption through blood. For who could measure his benefits with a worthy measure? With fatherly kindness he is always at work even in this, that what we believe we repay with our own blood is itself bestowed on us by almighty God. To him be glory for ever and ever. Amen.
